newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatian police question editor on Tudjman article.
newsitem.headline: Croatian police question editor on Tudjman article.

text.p: Croatian police questioned the editor of an independent magazine on Friday, a week after President Franjo Tudjman suggested he would clamp down on "false prophets...who preach human rights and media freedom."

The incident came a week after the government tried to close the influential radio station 101 in a move which sparked protests in the capital and drew criticism from Western governments. Zagreb subsequently reversed its decision.
The editor of the political bi-weekly Arkzin, Vesna Jankovic, said she believed her questioning by police was linked to Tujdman's announcement a week ago.
Jankovic said the authorities had objected to an article giving estimates of assets acquired by Tudjman's family since 1991.
A public prosecutor launched the investigation under a new libel law protecting the country's five top officials, who can instruct the state prosecutor to press charges.

"This marks the beginning of persecution. I am afraid non-governmental organisations and civic groups, which tried to preserve the citizen's conscience will now come under attack," Jankovic told Reuters.
On returning home from Washington on Saturday, Tudjman vowed in a speech to clamp down on those he said were linked, among other things, with the "enemies of Croatian independence".
"They are also linking up with fundamental extremists and false prophets of pseudo-democratic illusionists, who are today preaching great ideas about human rights and media freedom," Tudjman said.
Earlier this year, the editor and a journalist from a popular satirical weekly, the Feral Tribune, went on trial for defaming Tudjman, but were acquitted after intense international pressure.
The Council of Europe shelved Croatia's bid for admission in May, partly due to its treatment of the independent media. The country was accepted in November but remains under scrutiny.
Arkzin is a small magazine with a circulation of about 8,000 copies and is partly funded by the Soros Foundation, run by American tycoon George Soros.
